title: Linux basics
description: Move around the filesystem, manage files, search text, control processes and automate with scripts.

body.text: Everything in Linux lives in one tree of folders that starts at the root, written as a single slash: /.
Where am I?
Your shell always has a current folder, called the working directory. pwd (print working directory) shows it.
What is here?
ls lists the contents of a folder. Add -l for details and -a to include hidden files, whose names start with a dot.
Moving around
cd changes the working directory. cd .. goes up one level, and cd ~ (or just cd) returns to your home folder.
A path starting with / is absolute (from the root). Any other path is relative to where you are now.
A few short commands cover most everyday file work.

body.code:
mkdir notes          # make a folder
touch todo.txt       # make an empty file
cat todo.txt         # print a file
cp todo.txt copy.txt # copy
mv copy.txt old.txt  # move or rename
rm old.txt           # delete

body.text: Writing text into a file
echo prints text. The > sign sends that text into a file and replaces what was there. >> adds to the end instead.

body.code:
echo "buy milk" > todo.txt
echo "fix bug" >> todo.txt

body.text: rm does not use a recycle bin. A deleted file is gone, so read the command twice before pressing Enter.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the folder you are currently in?
questions.explanation: pwd prints the working directory. ls lists files, cd changes folder and whoami shows your user name.

questions.prompt: Which ls flag also shows hidden files such as .bashrc?
questions.explanation: -a means all, including names that start with a dot. -l shows details, -h makes sizes human readable and -r reverses the order.

questions.prompt: echo "hi" > notes.txt adds a line to the end of notes.txt.
questions.explanation: A single > replaces the whole file. Use >> to add to the end.

questions.prompt: Type the command that moves you up one folder.
questions.explanation: Two dots mean the parent folder, so cd .. goes up one level.

questions.prompt: Type the command that creates a folder called logs.
questions.explanation: mkdir makes a directory. The -p flag is optional here; it also creates missing parent folders.

questions.prompt: rm moves a deleted file to a recycle bin, so you can get it back later.
questions.explanation: The command line has no recycle bin. rm deletes the file for good, so check the name before pressing Enter.

labs.title: Find your way around
labs.scenario: You just logged in to a new server. Check where you are, move into the projects folder and make a place for your notes.
hints: Start by asking the shell where you are. The command name is short for print working directory.
Use cd to move into the projects folder, then mkdir to create a new folder.
Type: pwd, then cd projects, then mkdir notes

labs.title: Write a to-do list
labs.scenario: Create a to-do file, put two tasks in it, then keep a backup copy.
hints: echo with > creates a file and writes into it in one step.
Write a line containing the word deploy, then copy the file with cp.
Type: echo "deploy the app" > todo.txt, then cp todo.txt todo.bak

lessons.title: Who can read, write and run

body.text: Every file has three permission sets: for its owner, its group and everyone else. Each set can allow read (r), write (w) and execute (x).

body.caption: Owner can read and write, others can only read

body.text: Numbers instead of letters
Read is 4, write is 2 and execute is 1. Add them for each set: 7 means rwx, 5 means r-x and 4 means r--.
755 is the usual setting for scripts: you can edit and run them, everyone else can read and run them.

questions.prompt: What does chmod 755 give the file's owner?
questions.explanation: The first digit is for the owner. 7 = 4 + 2 + 1, which is read, write and execute.

questions.prompt: A script needs the execute (x) permission before you can run it with ./script.sh.
questions.explanation: Without x, the shell refuses with Permission denied. chmod +x or chmod 755 adds it.

questions.prompt: Type the command that makes deploy.sh executable.
questions.explanation: +x adds execute permission. chmod 755 deploy.sh works too.

questions.prompt: A file shows -rw-r----- in ls -l. What can users who are not the owner or in the group do?
questions.explanation: The last three characters (---) are for everyone else: no read, no write, no execute.

labs.title: Make a script runnable
labs.scenario: A teammate left a deploy script that will not run. Fix its permissions.
hints: Look at the long listing of the file to see its current permissions.
ls -l shows permissions. chmod changes them; 755 lets the owner read, write and run it.

body.text: Logs and config files are plain text. grep prints only the lines that contain a word, so you can find the one error in thousands of lines.

body.code:
grep ERROR app.log      # lines with ERROR
grep -i error app.log   # ignore upper or lower case
grep -c ERROR app.log   # count the matching lines
grep -v DEBUG app.log   # lines WITHOUT DEBUG

body.text: Pipes
The pipe | sends the output of one command into the next one. Small tools combine into powerful ones.

body.code:
cat app.log | grep ERROR | wc -l
history | grep docker
body.caption: Count errors, or find a command you typed earlier

body.text: Big files
head shows the first lines of a file and tail the last ones. -n picks how many. New log lines are added at the end, so tail is where problems usually are.
Save any result with a redirect: grep ERROR app.log > errors.txt

questions.prompt: What does the | sign do in cat app.log | grep ERROR?
options: Sends the output of cat into grep
Runs both commands on different files
Saves the output in a file called grep
correctAnswers: Sends the output of cat into grep
questions.explanation: A pipe connects commands: the output of the left one becomes the input of the right one.

questions.prompt: Type a command that counts the lines containing ERROR in app.log.
questions.explanation: grep -c counts matching lines. grep ERROR app.log | wc -l gives the same number.

questions.prompt: grep -i error finds lines with Error and ERROR.
questions.explanation: -i ignores the difference between upper and lower case.

questions.prompt: Which command shows the last lines of server.log?
questions.explanation: tail prints the end of a file (10 lines by default). head prints the beginning.

labs.title: Find the errors
labs.scenario: The web app crashed last night. Look at the end of the log, count the error lines, and save them to errors.txt in your home folder for the team.

files.content:

08:05:12 INFO  user alice logged in
08:07:40 DEBUG cache warmed
09:15:03 WARN  slow query: 2.4 s
10:02:55 ERROR payment service timed out
10:03:10 INFO  retrying payment
10:03:41 ERROR payment service timed out
11:20:00 INFO  user bob logged in

hints: The log is in the logs folder. tail shows the last lines of a file.
grep ERROR finds the error lines. Add -c to count them, and use > to save them into a file.
Type: tail logs/app.log, then grep -c ERROR logs/app.log, then grep ERROR logs/app.log > errors.txt

body.text: Every running program is a process. Each one has a number called its PID (process ID).

body.code:
ps        # programs in this terminal
ps aux    # every process on the machine

body.text: In ps aux the %CPU column shows how busy a process keeps the processor. A program stuck in a loop sits near 100%.
Stopping a process
kill PID politely asks a process to stop (the TERM signal). Most programs clean up and exit.

body.code:
kill 2210
kill -9 2210   # force it (the KILL signal)

body.text: A stuck program may ignore the polite request. kill -9 cannot be ignored, but the program gets no chance to save its work, so try plain kill first.
pgrep python prints the PID for you, and pkill python stops by name. You can only stop your own processes; root's need sudo.

questions.prompt: What is a PID?
options: The number of a running process
The folder a program lives in
correctAnswers: The number of a running process
questions.explanation: PID means process ID. Commands like kill use it to pick the process.

questions.prompt: kill -9 gives the program time to save its work before it stops.
questions.explanation: -9 sends KILL, which stops the program at once. Plain kill (TERM) is the polite way that lets it clean up.

questions.prompt: Type the command that lists every process on the machine.
questions.explanation: ps alone shows only this terminal. ps aux (or ps -ef) shows everything.

labs.title: Stop a runaway program
labs.scenario: The server is slow. One program is using almost all of the CPU. Find it and stop it, without touching anything else.
hints: ps aux lists every process. Look at the %CPU column.
Use grep or pgrep to find the PID of backup.py, then kill it. If it is still there afterwards, it ignored you: force it with -9.
Type: ps aux, then ps aux | grep backup, then kill -9 2210

body.text: A shell script is a text file full of commands. Running it types them for you, in order, the same way every time. That is the heart of automation.

body.code:
#!/bin/bash
# make a release folder and mark it ready
mkdir -p release
echo ready > release/status.txt
body.caption: deploy.sh

body.text: The first line, #!/bin/bash, tells Linux which program reads the script. Other lines starting with # are comments.
Running it
Run it with bash deploy.sh, or make it executable once and run it by its path.
./ means in this folder. Without it the shell only looks in the system's program folders.
There is no text editor in this app, so build a script line by line: echo "mkdir -p release" > deploy.sh, then add lines with >>.

questions.prompt: Why do you type ./deploy.sh instead of deploy.sh?
options: ./ says the script is in the current folder
correctAnswers: ./ says the script is in the current folder
questions.explanation: The shell looks for bare names only in system folders. ./ points at the current folder.

questions.prompt: A script needs execute permission before you can run it as ./script.sh.
questions.explanation: Without x permission you get Permission denied. bash script.sh still works, because bash only reads the file.

questions.prompt: Type the command that runs backup.sh with bash.
questions.explanation: bash reads the file and runs its lines. sh backup.sh works too.

labs.title: Automate a release
labs.scenario: Write a small deploy script that creates a release folder and writes a status file into it. Make it executable and run it.
hints: Build the script with echo: > creates the file, >> adds a line. It needs a mkdir line and a line that writes release/status.txt.
Then chmod +x deploy.sh and run it with ./deploy.sh.
Type: echo "mkdir -p release" > deploy.sh, then echo "echo ready > release/status.txt" >> deploy.sh, then chmod +x deploy.sh, then ./deploy.sh
